newsitem.title: USA: Nothing "derogatory" found about missing US pilot.
newsitem.headline: Nothing "derogatory" found about missing US pilot.

text.p: An Air Force investigation into the background of a pilot missing with his bomb-laden warplane in the Rocky Mountains has found no evidence to explain why he disappeared, a spokesman said Monday.

"There is no derogatory evidence," Lt. Gen. Frank Campbell of Davis-Monthan Air Force Base told a news briefing in Eagle, Colorado. He was responding to suggestions that the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, may have committed suicide by crashing his A-10 Thunderbolt in the snow-covered mountains of Colorado.

"We have still uncovered no evidence to help find the pilot or the plane," Campbell told reporters. He said investigators had carried out some 200 interviews with people "about the past of Captain Button," who disappeared 12 days ago while piloting his plane on a training mission.
On New York's Long Island, Button's father was quoted on CNN as saying his 32-year-old son was not suicidal and was "an honest and devoted" flyer.

Search efforts resumed Monday in the mountains of central Colorado for any sign of the plane, but one pilot told CNN the search was harder than looking for a needle in a haystack. "It's covered with three feet of snow, so you have to find the haystack first," the pilot said.

Rescue workers using radar images and photos taken by U-2 and SR-71 Blackbird reconnaissance aircraft narrowed the search to an area near the Vail ski area. Button's A-10 disappeared on April 2 while flying in a three-aircraft formation on a routine training mission in Arizona.
Air Force officials are at a loss to explain why Button apparently veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles (1,350 km) from where the training exercise was taking place.

Defence officials said the plane, carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) conventional Mark 82 bombs, disappeared from the rear of the formation after leaving Davis-Monthan Air Force Base near Tucson, Arizona.
